paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.49:1 Rule 14.49 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.49. In Carbone v. McMahon, 2015 ABCA 263, the appellant unsuccessfully applied for an extension of the time to file an appeal. The respondent did not file a memorandum in opposition to the application. Justice Slatter declined to award the successful respondent costs of the application. His Lordship said: 12 The respondents did not file a memorandum in opposition to this application, as contemplated by R. 14.41. As a consequence, the respondents had no right to make oral submissions: [Rule 14.49]. This rule is intended to enable the Court and the parties to properly prepare for the application, to reduce the time required to hear the application, and to avoid surprise and adjournments. The respondents were therefore only permitted to indicate that the application was opposed. In the circumstances, there will be no costs of this application.

paragraphs.text: A memorandum filed on an application (a) must be formatted in the same manner as a factum under rule 14.26(1), (b) must not be longer than (i) 10 double-spaced pages for an application for permission to appeal, or (ii) 5 double-spaced pages for any other application, (c) may in addition attach a chronology, where that is relevant to the application, and (d) in an application for permission to appeal, must (i) include a copy of the reasons for the decision proposed to be appealed, and (ii) state the exact questions of law on which permission to appeal is requested. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.54:1 Rule 14.54 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.54. 1. — Exact questions of law In Legacy Inc. Red Deer (City), 2018 ABCA 393, 2018 CarswellAlta 3011, 79 Alta. L.R. (6th) 1, 81 M.P.L.R. (5th) 181, Justice Wakeling discussed the requirement that an applicant's memorandum of argument state the exact questions of law for which permission to appeal is sought. His Lordship said: [67] Rule 14.54(c)(ii) of the Alberta Rules of Court states that an applicant's memorandum of argument filed in support of an application for permission to appeal “must state the exact questions of law on which permission to appeal is requested”. [68] Adherence to this rule ensures that both the respondent and the court are aware from the outset of the precise question or questions that the applicant seeks leave to present to the Court of Appeal. [69] Advance notice ensures that the respondent is not taken by surprise and is able to effectively utilize its opportunity to file a memorandum of argument and to present oral argument and, generally, to participate meaningfully in the permission-to-appeal process. If the respondent and the court do not know what the applicant's target is, it is difficult to argue or determine that the applicant has missed the mark. [70] Rule compliance also benefits the judge. It relieves the judge of the obligation to search the applicant's permission-to-appeal application and memorandum of argument for a clear statement of the legal questions the applicant wants permission to argue before a panel of the court.[44] [71] Finally, failure to honor this rule may diminish the value of oral argument. If the court allows the parties to file supplemental material, the court will, in effect, be deprived of the benefit of oral argument based on the parties' second memorandum of argument. A judge, keenly aware of the additional costs a second hearing would impose on the parties, would be extremely reluctant to call counsel back for the sole purpose of addressing the subject matter of the supplementary material. [72] The applicant also derives a benefit from rule-compliant conduct. A clear statement in its memorandum of argument of the questions it wishes to have resolved reduces the likelihood that the court will draft the questions. There is always the risk that the court will not pose the question the same way that counsel would.[45] A good lawyer always wants to have control of the pen.[46] [73] A court may consider questions that were not set out in the applicant's initial memorandum of argument if this will not cause the respondent unreasonable prejudice. [74] There are two distinct components of unreasonable prejudice. [75] First, the respondent may suffer unreasonable prejudice if it has not been afforded a reasonable opportunity to respond to the applicant's new questions. This may exist if the applicant has not clearly stated the new questions of law or jurisdiction that it wishes to have the Court of Appeal address or the respondent has not had sufficient time to compose its reply or both. [76] Second, the respondent will suffer unreasonable prejudice if the applicant's failure to comply with r. 14.54(c)(ii) of the Alberta Rules of Court caused the respondent to incur additional legal costs that it would not have had the applicant complied with r. 14.54(c)(ii) and presented “the exact questions of law” in its first memorandum of argument. A court may remedy this harm by ordering the applicant to wholly or partially indemnify the respondent for the additional legal costs the applicant's noncompliant conduct has caused the respondent to incur. [77] Appellate courts, for good reason, are reluctant to resolve an issue that a party did not present to the original tribunal—either a court or a statutory delegate. “The general rule … is that a new issue may not be raised on appeal”.[47] [78] I have explained why before:[48] The first reason reflects a fear that the failure of a disputant to flag a contentious point at earlier stages of the litigation spectrum may adversely affect the appeal court's ability to make a fully informed decision. The factual foundation may be absent. Or failure to present the argument to the original adjudicator may deprive the appeal court of the perspective of the decision maker whose assessment is under review. … The second reason acknowledges that in some circumstances late presentation of an argument may prejudice the adversary. This certainly is a very real risk if the adversary would have supplemented the record had it known another issue was before the court. There may be other reasons why an adversary is prejudiced. [79] A court may grant an applicant permission to raise questions of law or jurisdiction that were not argued before a board if neither the administration of justice nor the respondent will suffer unreasonable prejudice. [80] The administration of justice will suffer unreasonable prejudice if the panel of the court hearing the appeal would be deprived of important insights a board alone may be able to offer or a necessary factual foundation is missing. The Municipal Government Act contemplates that the vast majority of development issues will be resolved by a board consisting of members representative of different community interests. A court may be reluctant to adopt a procedure that eliminates this community voice. [81] A respondent may suffer unreasonable prejudice if it would have presented additional specific evidence had it been forewarned the new question was a live issue.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.57:1 Rule 14.57 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.57. 1. Test In Ravvin v. Canada Bread Company, 2020 ABCA 287, 2020 CarswellAlta 1410, a person applied to be added as a respondent to the appeal before the Court. The Court said: [4] Cases such as Carbon Development Partnership v Alberta (Energy and Utilities Board), 2007 ABCA 231, para 9, and Hayes v Mayhood (1958), 1958 CanLII 549 (AB QB), 24 WWR (ns) 332, 335 (Alta CA), aff'd 1959 CanLII 72 (SCC), [1959] SCR 568, 18 DLR (2d) 497, indicate that the Court may exercise its necessarily implied power to add parties if the applicant has a legal interest in the outcome of the proceeding and it is in the interests of justice to do so, and the Court may also add parties to an appeal under the Rules of Court: HE v APEGA Appeal Board, 2019 ABCA 298, paras 13-14. … [6] The current application is made pursuant to rules 14.57 and 3.74(2)(b). [7] The applicant must first show it has a legal interest in the outcome of the proceedings. If so, there are two sub-tests: whether it is just and convenient to add the applicant, and whether the applicant's interest can be adequately protected only if it is granted party status: Saskatchewan Power Corporation v NaturEner USA, LLC, 2014 ABCA 318, para 10. In HE v. APEGA Appeal Board, 2019 ABCA 298, 2019 CarswellAlta 1650, an engineer, as a member of the Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of Alberta (APEGA), was investigated and prosecuted by APEGA's Investigative Committee on allegations of unprofessional conduct. The Discipline Committee of APEGA found the engineer guilty. APEGA's Appeal Board substantially upheld the Discipline Committee's findings. The engineer appealed to the Court of Appeal. The Appeal Board (which was required by statute to be named as a respondent in the appeal) applied to have the Investigative Committee added as a respondent. Justice Khullar granted the application, and said: [4] The engineer appellant opposes the application on the basis that s 70(2) only requires that the Appeal Board be named, therefore no one else should be named. Further, since the entire record will be available to the Court, the position of the Investigative Committee will be before the Court. [5] The basic argument for this application is that, as an adjudicative tribunal whose decision is under appeal, the Appeal Board's participation in the appeal is narrowly circumscribed by cases like Northwestern Utilities Ltd v City of Edmonton, 1978 CanLII 17 (SCC), [1979] 1 SCR 684 and Leon's Furniture Limited v Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner), 2011 ABCA 94 (CanLII). These cases have been understood as prohibiting an adjudicative tribunal from making arguments in support of its own decision in a judicial review or a statutory appeal. Their submissions are usually limited to topics like jurisdiction, standard of review and clarification of the record. [6] This rule has been relaxed somewhat since Ontario (Energy Board) v Ontario Power Generation Inc., 2015 SCC 44 (CanLII) but the Appeal Board submits that the restrictive approach continues to apply to purely adjudicative bodies. [7] A consequence of the limitation on the Appeal Board's participation is that, if this appeal were to proceed with only the currently named parties, this Court would have to decide the appeal without an adversarial context. [8] The proposed solution to this problem is for this Court to add the Investigative Committee as a respondent. The Investigative Committee was the party opposite the engineer appellant in all previous proceedings. Further, the Investigative Committee is not an adjudicative body, so would not be prohibited from arguing the merits of the Appeal Board's decision. [9] The Investigative Committee's function is to investigate complaints against APEGA members and prosecute the disciplinary matters that proceed to a hearing before the Discipline Committee. In this case, the Investigative Committee argued the unprofessional conduct charge and appropriate sanction before the Discipline Committee. When the engineer appealed the Discipline Committee's decision to the Appeal Board, the Investigative Committee defended the Discipline Committee's decision and successfully cross appealed the award of costs. [10] I am satisfied that providing an adversarial context for the panel that hears this appeal strongly favours adding the Investigative Committee as a respondent. The Investigative Committee's general function and its particular role in the proceedings below indicate that it is well-positioned and likely the only party to make arguments responding to this appeal. The engineer appellant's argument that the Investigative Committee's position will be before the Court through the record is akin to arguing that the Crown need not be a party to an appeal as its position will be apparent to the Court from the trial record. The adversarial process also applies to appeals.

sentences.text: Intervenor status on appeal

paragraphs.text: (1) In addition to persons having a right to intervene in law, a single appeal judge may grant status to a person to intervene in an appeal, subject to any terms and conditions and with the rights and privileges specified by the judge. (2) A person granted intervenor status in the court appealed from must apply again to obtain intervenor status on an appeal. (2) A person granted intervenor status in the court appealed from must apply again to obtain intervenor status on an appeal.

(7th) 309, Justice Wakeling said, at paragraphs 8–10: [8] My review of the case law on intervention leads me to conclude that the following proposition is sound: A single appeal judge may[6] grant permission to intervene in an appeal if satisfied that the applicant (a) will be directly and significantly affected[7] by the outcome of the appeal or (b) has special expertise or perspective[8] relating to the subject matter of the appeal[9] that will assist the Court in its deliberations.[10] [9] The Supreme Court of Canada has declared that the “purpose of an intervention is to present the court with submissions which are useful and different from the perspective of a non-party who has a special interest or particular expertise in the subject matter of the appeal”.[11] As Justice Major stated, “The implied promise of the intervener is that intervention will be useful and different from the submission of the appellant and respondent”. “Interveners and the Supreme Court of Canada”, May 1999 National 27. An applicant who can enhance the Court's understanding of the competing interests is an excellent candidate for intervenor status. [10] A court must be reluctant to decline assistance from an organization whose members are major participants in a business or other sector that will be directly affected by the Court's decision and would be in a position to address the implications of different potential solutions.[12] At the same time, a court must not be oblivious to the fact that an intervenor most likely will increase the private and public costs of the litigation.[13] A balanced assessment of these conflicting values is required. 1. Intervenor Status This is an application for intervenor status by the National ME/FM Action Network, which is a group of persons whose members have been diagnosed with myalgic encephalomyelitis or fibromyalgia. The purpose of the intervention, we are told, would be to assist the Court in coming to the conclusion that the trial judge whose decision [(1994), 21 Alta. L.R. (3d) 11; additional reasons 23 Alta. The difficulty with the position of the applicant is this: in order to get intervention status before this Court, one has to be able to demonstrate, inter alia, that the decision this Court might make in this case might adversely affect the applicant because we would adopt a rule of law that would adversely affect the applicant. Ms. Morgan has argued most eloquently today that the decision under appeal, which was widely reported in the media, has adversely affected the members of the applicant group because they have since been challenged—in various settings—about the validity of their medical condition. An example was given of persons who suddenly are challenged about disability insurance benefits. The difficulty is that any problem like that will not be resolved one way or the other by this appeal. The reason for that is that we will not, in this appeal, and as a matter of law, say that there is or is not such a thing as fibromyalgia. That is not our function. The function of the Court hearing the appeal will be to decide whether or not the trial judge in this case made reasonable findings of fact based on the evidence before her… In our view, the application must fail because there is no possibility that we will adopt any rule of law that will adversely affect the applicants. Canada (Attorney General) (2005), 380 A.R. 301 (C.A.), Chief Justice Fraser made the following comments concerning the granting of intervenor status (at pp. 303–305): It may be fairly stated that, as a general principle, an intervention may be allowed where the proposed intervener is specially affected by the decision facing the Court or the proposed intervener has some special expertise or insight to bring to bear on the issues facing the court. As explained by the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. Morgentaler, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 462, 157 N.R. 97, 125 N.S.R. (2d) 81, 349 A.P.R. 81, at para. 1: “[t]he purpose of an intervention is to present the court with submissions which are useful and different from the perspective of a non-party who has a special interest or particular expertise in the subject matter of the appeal.” That said, it is clear as noted by the Federal Court of Appeal in Corbiere et al. v. Canada (Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs) et al. (1996), 199 N.R. 1 (F.C.A.), that “… an intervenor in an appellate court must take the case as she finds it and cannot, to the prejudice of the parties, argue new issues which require the introduction of fresh evidence.” … A two-step approach is commonly used to determine an intervener application. The Court typically first considers the subject matter of the proceeding and second, determines the proposed intervener's interest in that subject matter. It is clear from reviewing the appellants' factum that there are three main issues on the appeal: 1. The tests for striking pleadings and summary judgment and, in particular, whether summary judgment is appropriate for resolution of complex evidentiary and novel legal issues based on aboriginal and treaty rights. 2. Whether the appellants lack standing to assert claims based on aboriginal and treaty rights because they are not a band. This, in turn, involves a number of potential issues including treaty rights under Treaty 6 and constitutional protection of treaty and aboriginal rights under s. 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982. 3. To what extent, if any, provincial limitation periods can be invoked to extinguish aboriginal or treaty rights. In cases involving constitutional issues or which have a constitutional dimension to them, courts are generally more lenient in granting intervener status: Trang et al. v. Edmonton Remand Centre (Director) et al., [2002] A.R. Uned. 109, [2002] 8 W.W.R. 755, 2002 ABQB 185 and Alberta Sports & Recreation Association for the Blind v. Edmonton (City), [1994] 2 W.W.R. 659 (Q.B.). Similarly, appellate courts are more willing to consider intervener applications than courts of first instance. As noted by Hugessen J. in Bellegarde et al. v. Canada (Attorney General) (2002), 223 F.T.R. 60, 2002 FCT 1001: …[T]he test for allowing intervener standing for argument at the appellate level is necessarily different from that which is used at trial; trials must remain manageable and the parties must be able to define the issues and the evidence on which they will be decided. An appellate court on the other hand deals with a pre-established record that is not normally subject to change. And an appellate court, while benefiting from the different viewpoints expressed by interveners, is far better equipped to limit and control the length and nature of their interventions. … In constitutional cases, if an applicant can show its interests will be affected by the outcome of the litigation, intervener status should be granted: Skapinker v. Law Society of Upper Canada (1984), 53 N.R. 169, 3 O.A.C. 321, 9 D.L.R. (4th) 161 (S.C.C.). Or, as already noted, if the intervener applicant possesses some expertise which might be of assistance to the court in resolving the issues before it, that too will do. As explained by Brian Crane in Practice and Advocacy in the Supreme Court, (British Columbia Continuing Legal Education Seminar, 1983), at p. 1.1.05, and approved by the Supreme Court of Canada in Reference Re Sections 32 and 34 of the Worker's Compensation Act (Nfld.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 335, 96 N.R. 231, 76 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 185, 235 A.P.R. 185, at 340: an intervention is welcomed if the intervener will provide the Court with fresh information or a fresh perspective on an important constitutional or public issue. In Orphan Well Assn. v. Grant Thornton Ltd., 2016 ABCA 238, 2016 CarswellAlta 1466, Justice Sheilah Martin gave this summary of the law regarding intervenor status: 7 Rules 14.37(2) and 14.58 of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, authorize a single appeal judge to grant permission to a party to intervene in an appeal and impose conditions on the intervention. The intervener cannot raise or argue novel issues on appeal unless otherwise permitted: Rule 14.58(3). 8 Granting intervener status is a two-step process. The court first considers the subject matter of the appeal and then determines the proposed intervener's interest in it: Papaschase Indian Band (Descendants of) v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320 at para 5, 380 AR 301. In determining a proposed intervener's interest, a court should examine (a) if the intervener will be directly and significantly affected by the appeal's outcome, and (b) if the intervener will provide some expertise or fresh perspective on the subject matter that will be helpful in resolving the appeal. 9 Papaschase stated parties could be granted intervener status if they met either criterion. However, subsequent decisions have set out that simply establishing an affected interested is not enough to grant leave. A proposed intervener must also provide fresh information or a fresh perspective: Pedersen v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 192 at para 10, 432 AR 219. If parties can intervene simply because they have affected interests, the number of potential interveners would greatly increase and unduly delay the appeal process without a corresponding benefit. 10 In Pedersen, this court stated (at para 3) that the following questions are relevant factors to consider when determining whether to grant intervener status: 1. Will the intervener be directly affected by the appeal; 2. Is the presence of the intervener necessary for the court to properly decide the matter; 3. Might the intervener's interest in the proceedings not be fully protected by the parties; 4. Will the intervener's submission be useful and different or bring particular expertise to the subject matter of the appeal; 5. Will the intervention unduly delay the proceedings; 6. Will there possibly be prejudice to the parties if intervention is granted; 7. Will intervention widen the lis between the parties; and 8. Will the intervention transform the court into a political arena? 11 The power to allow interveners is discretionary and should be exercised sparingly: R v Neve (1996), 1996 ABCA 242 at para 16, 184 AR 359. However, interveners have been allowed when they add significantly to complex constitutional issues, especially those, like the case at bar, with serious and wide ranging policy implications. 12 As explained in R v Morgentaler, [1993] 1 SCR 462 (SCC) at para 1, “[t]he purpose of an intervention is to present the court with submissions which are useful and different from the perspective of a non-party who has a special interest or particular expertise in the subject matter of the appeal.” 13 The court's ability to assess whether an intervener has something useful and different to add is tied to how clearly the intervener articulates the submissions they seek to advance. A bare assertion that one has a unique perspective is far less helpful than an overview of the arguments the intervener seeks to advance. The Supreme Court requires applicants to identify the position of the intervener intends to take, set out the submissions to be advanced, the questions on which they propose to intervene, their relevance to the proceeding and the reasons for believing that the submissions will be useful to the Court and different from those of the other parties. See rule 57(2) of the Rules of the Supreme Court of Canada, SOR/83-74. This level of specificity is to be encouraged in this court as well. 2. Test for Leave to Intervene In R. v. Vallentgoed, 2016 ABCA 19, Justice Veldhuis said: 4 Rules 14.37(2) and 14.58 of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, gives authority to a single appeal judge to grant leave to a party to intervene in an appeal and impose conditions on the intervention. The intervener cannot raise or argue novel issues on appeal: Rule 14.58(3). 5 Intervener status will be granted where the applicant: (1) is directly and significantly affected by the outcome of the appeal, and (2) has expertise and a fresh perspective on the subject matter of the appeal that is useful for the appeal's resolution: R v Morgentaler, [1993] 1 SCR 462 at para 1, [1993] SCJ No 48 (QL); City of Edmonton v Edmonton (Subdivision and Development Appeal Board), 2014 ABCA 340 at para 8, 584 AR 255. The factors that inform these two questions include (Pedersen v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 192 at para 3, 432 AR 219; Re Stewart Estate, 2014 ABCA 222 at para 5, 577 AR 57): 1. Will the intervener be directly affected by the appeal; 2. Is the presence of the intervener necessary for the Court to properly decide the matter; 3. Might the intervener's interest in the proceedings not be fully protected by the parties; 4. Will the intervener's submission be useful and different or bring particular expertise to the subject matter of the appeal; 5. Will the intervention unduly delay the proceedings; 6. Will there possibly be prejudice to the parties if intervention is granted; 7. Will intervention widen the lis between the parties; and 8. Will the intervention transform the Court into a political arena? 6 The discretion to grant intervener status should be exercised sparingly, particularly in criminal proceedings where the dispute must remain between the accused and the Crown: R v Neve, [1996] 8 WWR 294 at para 16, 184 AR 359 (CA). Interventions in criminal appeals are “generally shunned by the courts for a variety of policy and prudential reasons”, especially the risk “that the hearing of other voices can distort an appeal”: R v JLA, 2009 ABCA 324 at para 2, 464 AR 310. In Orphan Well Assn. v. Grant Thorton Ltd., 2016 ABCA 238, 2016 CarswellAlta 1466, see annotation under 1. Intervenor Status. See also: Styles v. Alberta Investment Management Corp., 2016 ABCA 218, 2016 CarswellAlta 1371 at paragraphs 13–15. See also: Canadian Centre for Bio-Ethical Reform v. Grande Prairie (City), 2017 ABCA 280, 2017 CarswellAlta 1571 at paragraphs 8–11. In AC and JF v. Alberta, 2020 ABCA 309, 2020 CarswellAlta 1571, the Court said: [8] Under Rules 14.37(2)(e) and 14.58 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, a single appeal judge has authority to grant permission to intervene in an appeal and to impose conditions on the intervention. [9] All parties to these applications agree on the test for permission to intervene. I must consider (1) whether the proposed intervenor has a particular interest in, or will be directly and significantly affected by the outcome of the appeal, or (2) whether the intervenor will provide some special expertise, perspective, or information that will help resolve the appeal: Edmonton (City) v Urban Development Institute, 2014 ABCA 340 at para 8; Hamm v Canada (Attorney General), 2019 ABCA 389 at para 5; Papaschase Indian Band No 136 v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320 at para 5 [Papaschase]. [10] Other relevant considerations include: 1. Is the presence of the intervenor necessary for the court to properly decide the matter? 2. Might the intervenor's interest in the proceedings not be fully protected by the parties? 3. Will the intervention unduly delay the proceedings? 4. Will there be possible prejudice to the parties if intervention is granted? 5. Will intervention widen the dispute between the parties? 6. Will the intervention transform the court into a political arena? 7. Will the intervener's submission be useful and different or bring particular expertise to the subject matter of the appeal? UAlberta Pro-Life v Governors of the University of Alberta, 2018 ABCA 350 at para 10; Pederson v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 192 at para 3. [11] With respect to the scope of intervenor submissions, the case law establishes there are no bright lines precluding an intervenor from raising issues and argument not raised below. If the proposed new issues or arguments require fresh evidence or prejudice a party, they are likely impermissible: Papaschase at para 3 citing Batchewana Indian Band v Canada (Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs (1996), 199 NR 1. Even absent the need for fresh evidence or possible prejudice, it is not “appropriate for an intervener to extend legal argument well beyond what the courts below and the parties have advanced”: Deloitte & Touche v Ontario, 2003 SCC 61 at para 31. Courts should be guided by the causes of action in the pleadings. So, for example, an intervenor should not be permitted to raise constitutional issues where no constitutional issues have been raised in the pleadings: Johnston v Alberta (Vital Statistics), 2008 ABCA 2 at para 7. However, arguing a new point inextricably linked to an issue the parties have already put before the court is permissible. An example of this is found in Alberta (Minister of Justice) v Métis Settlements Appeal Tribunal, 2005 ABCA 143, at para 9, where the intervenor was permitted to argue the potential application of s 25 of the Charter as it was inextricably linked to other sections of the Charter already in issue. [12] The Supreme Court of Canada said at para 40 of Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada (Minister of Canadian Heritage), 2005 SCC 69 that “an intervenor is in no worse a position than a party who belatedly discovers some legal argument that it ought to have raised earlier in the proceedings but did not.” An intervenor may always “put forward any legal argument in support of what it submits is the correct legal conclusion on an issue properly before the Court, provided that in doing so its legal argument does not require additional facts”: Mikisew at para 40. In Wesley v. Alberta, 2023 ABCA 289, the Court of Appeal noted that the factors of “particular interest in the outcome of the appeal” and “special expertise” do not create an “either/or” situation; both factors should be considered in an application for intervenor status. At paragraph 8, the Court said: [8] More recently, in VLM v Dominey Estate, 2023 ABCA 226, Slatter JA noted that the test for intervention “is based on (1) whether the proposed intervenor has a particular interest in, or will be directly and significantly affected by the outcome of the appeal, or (2) whether the intervenor will provide some special expertise, perspective, or information that will help resolve the appeal”: para 2. An intervenor “does not have to satisfy both branches of the test… intervenor status does not automatically follow from showing either an ‘interest’ or a ‘fresh perspective’. The test is not strictly conjunctive or disjunctive, but rather involves a consideration of both factors in all cases”: para 3. 3. Applications to Intervene on an Application to Seek Leave to Appeal In Balancing Pool v. ENMAX Energy Corporation, 2018 ABCA 143, 2018 CarswellAlta 698, the Alberta Utilities Commission issued a ruling after a hearing, and some of the parties (“predecessor STS contract holders”) in that hearing applied for leave to appeal the AUC's decision to the Court of Appeal. Balancing Pool (and others) applied to Justice Paperny for an order adding them as parties or, alternatively, intervenors, to the application for leave to appeal made by the predecessor STS contract holders. In ruling on the application, Justice Paperny discussed applications to add parties or intervenors to applications for leave to appeal. Her Ladyship said: 20 This Court has an inherent power to add parties to an appeal should it find that it is in the interests of justice to do so: Hayes v Mayhood et al, [1959] SCR 568, 18 DLR (2d) 497. The guiding principles have been set forth in Carbon Development Partnership v Alberta (Energy and Utilities Board), 2007 ABCA 231, [2007] A.J. No. 727 (QL) at para 9: This court has inherent power to add parties to an appeal, especially if an applicant's interests are not represented: … The joinder test is whether or not the applicant has a legal interest in the outcome of the proceeding. If so, there are two different sub-tests. The first is whether it is just and convenient to add the applicant. The second is whether or not the applicant's interest would only be adequately protected if it were granted party status. 21 However, this Court strongly discourages adding parties or allowing intervenors at this earlier stage, for the purpose of an application for permission to appeal. The reason for this is clear: in the absence of permission to appeal being granted, there is no appeal and as such no interest, legal or economic, that can be directly affected by the application (at least immediately). If the application to appeal is granted, parties are at liberty to apply for status at the hearing of the appeal. If the application is dismissed, there is no appeal. Unless and until permission is granted, proposed parties are not generally at risk. Usually the issues on a permission application are narrow and are focussed on the statutory requirements. In other words, the inquiry at that stage is usually a narrow one and rarely assisted by representations from multiple parties. 22 For these reasons, this Court has held that adding parties or intervenors should be discouraged at this stage of the proceedings absent extraordinary circumstances. As stated by Hunt JA in Carbon at para 6: Applications for intervener status in leave applications are rare. In the Board context, leave to appeal can only be granted if important questions of law or jurisdiction are raised: Alberta Energy and Utilities Board Act, R.S.A. 2000, C. A-17, s. 26(1) (“AEUB Act”). At this stage, it is unknown whether leave will be granted and, if so, on what questions. It is therefore extremely difficult to know what interests, if any, of the applicants may be affected and what, if anything, they may be able to contribute to the proceedings. This no doubt explains the wisdom behind the Supreme Court of Canada's practice to usually defer intervener applications until after leave has been granted, even if a party has enjoyed intervener status before the lower courts: R. v. N.M.P., 2000 SCC 59, [2000] 2 S.C.R. 857 at para. 5. An even stronger rational for awaiting the outcome of the leave applications may exist in regulatory proceedings like this where, if leave is granted, the questions will be limited in scope. 4. Costs In Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association Inc. v. Thomson, 2024 ABCA 43, the Association unsuccessfully sought intervenor status in an appeal dealing with the interpretation of a life insurance policy. The question arose: should the Association pay costs to the party which successfully opposed the application for intervenor status? Justice Pentelechuk discussed when costs might be awarded against intervenors (or those seeking intervenor status), and awarded costs against the Association. Her Ladyship said: [2] Indeed, the general rule that costs are neither awarded to nor against interveners is longstanding: see Harper v Harper, 1979 CanLII 168 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 2 at 16; Young v Young, 1993 CanLII 34 (SCC), [1993] 4 SCR 3 at 138; and B(R) v Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto, 1995 CanLII 115 (SCC), [1995] 1 SCR 315. B(R) was a case where the intervener in question was the Ontario Attorney General. The court was explicit about the rule relating to a “public intervener”, referring to an award of “costs against an intervening Attorney General, acting… in the public interest” being permitted “only in very rare cases” (para 122), “the rule that a party granted intervener status in the public interest is, generally, neither entitled to nor liable for the costs in the matter” (para 176) and “the general rule that costs not be awarded to or against an intervener in the public interest” (para 178). [3] It is clear from review of the case law that the court's discretion to award costs both to and against an intervener is not fettered by this general rule. [4] In Alberta, while this Court has acknowledged the general rule that an intervener should bear its own costs, it does not necessarily follow from such a general rule that an intervener should never be liable for costs. For instance, Slatter JA in Métis Nation of Alberta Association v Alberta (Indigenous Relations), 2022 ABCA 250 at para 17 held that while those granted intervener status are not entitled to costs of the appeal or the intervener applications, “[w]hether they are liable to pay costs will be in the discretion of the panel that hears the appeal” [emphasis added]. In Armcorp 4-18 Ltd (Bankruptcy of the Estates) v Canada, 1999 ABCA 95 at para 15, after dismissing the appeal this Court ordered the intervener, the Royal Bank of Canada, to pay costs of an intervention motion. [5] Historically, the general rule regarding costs has been tied to “public interest” interventions, often involving constitutional challenges. There are sound policy reasons for doing so, rooted in notions of access to justice and advocacy in matters of public importance. But many interventions seek to advance private interests. [6] The distinction between public and private interveners was explored in Incredible Electronics Inc v Canada (Attorney General) (2006), 2006 CanLII 17939 (ON SC), 80 OR (3d) 723 (SC). In Perell J's view, classifying the intervener's involvement as either public or private interest helps determine whether the intervener falls within or outside the normal rule that interveners neither receive nor pay costs. [7] I agree with this reasoning. Admittedly, there are no bright lines separating public interest interveners from those advancing private interests. Public interest interveners can have private interests also furthered by the intervention…. [8] Classifying the intervention as, or predominantly as, public interest or private interest is an important consideration in determining whether the general rule on costs should apply. Intervention applications are increasingly common. Some are successful, some are not, but when the interest advanced is a private one and the application is unsuccessful, there is no principled reason why the proposed intervener should not bear costs. Awarding costs in the appropriate case may also serve to mitigate against interventions that are nothing but “busybody” applications: see Wong v Giannacopoulos, 2011 ABCA 206 at para 10. …. [10] The Association is not a public interest litigant, rather it represents the majority of life insurers in Canada. The Association's proposed application was clearly made to further private interests.

As explained by Brian Crane in Practice and Advocacy in the Supreme Court, (British Columbia Continuing Legal Education Seminar, 1983), at p.
1.1.05, and approved by the Supreme Court of Canada in Reference Re Sections 32 and 34 of the Worker's Compensation Act (Nfld.), [1989] 2 S.C.R.
231, 76 Nfld. & P.E.I.R.
185, at 340: an intervention is welcomed if the intervener will provide the Court with fresh information or a fresh perspective on an important constitutional or public issue.
In Orphan Well Assn. v.

Grant Thornton Ltd., 2016 ABCA 238, 2016 CarswellAlta 1466, Justice Sheilah Martin gave this summary of the law regarding intervenor status: 7 Rules 14.37(2) and 14.58 of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, authorize a single appeal judge to grant permission to a party to intervene in an appeal and impose conditions on the intervention.
The intervener cannot raise or argue novel issues on appeal unless otherwise permitted: Rule 14.58(3).
8 Granting intervener status is a two-step process.

The court first considers the subject matter of the appeal and then determines the proposed intervener's interest in it: Papaschase Indian Band (Descendants of) v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320 at para 5, 380 AR 301.
In determining a proposed intervener's interest, a court should examine
(a) if the intervener will be directly and significantly affected by the appeal's outcome, and
(b) if the intervener will provide some expertise or fresh perspective on the subject matter that will be helpful in resolving the appeal.
9 Papaschase stated parties could be granted intervener status if they met either criterion.
However, subsequent decisions have set out that simply establishing an affected interested is not enough to grant leave.
A proposed intervener must also provide fresh information or a fresh perspective: Pedersen v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 192 at para 10, 432 AR 219.
If parties can intervene simply because they have affected interests, the number of potential interveners would greatly increase and unduly delay the appeal process without a corresponding benefit.
10 In Pedersen, this court stated (at para 3) that the following questions are relevant factors to consider when determining whether to grant intervener status: 1.
Will the intervener be directly affected by the appeal; 2.
Is the presence of the intervener necessary for the court to properly decide the matter; 3.
Might the intervener's interest in the proceedings not be fully protected by the parties; 4.
Will the intervener's submission be useful and different or bring particular expertise to the subject matter of the appeal; 5.
Will the intervention unduly delay the proceedings; 6.
Will there possibly be prejudice to the parties if intervention is granted; 7.
Will intervention widen the lis between the parties; and 8.
Will the intervention transform the court into a political arena?
11 The power to allow interveners is discretionary and should be exercised sparingly: R v Neve (1996), 1996 ABCA 242 at para 16, 184 AR 359.
However, interveners have been allowed when they add significantly to complex constitutional issues, especially those, like the case at bar, with serious and wide ranging policy implications.

12 As explained in R v Morgentaler, [1993] 1 SCR 462 (SCC) at para 1, “[t]he purpose of an intervention is to present the court with submissions which are useful and different from the perspective of a non-party who has a special interest or particular expertise in the subject matter of the appeal.” 13 The court's ability to assess whether an intervener has something useful and different to add is tied to how clearly the intervener articulates the submissions they seek to advance.
A bare assertion that one has a unique perspective is far less helpful than an overview of the arguments the intervener seeks to advance.

The Supreme Court requires applicants to identify the position of the intervener intends to take, set out the submissions to be advanced, the questions on which they propose to intervene, their relevance to the proceeding and the reasons for believing that the submissions will be useful to the Court and different from those of the other parties.
See rule 57(2) of the Rules of the Supreme Court of Canada, SOR/83-74.
This level of specificity is to be encouraged in this court as well.
Test for Leave to Intervene In R. v.

Vallentgoed, 2016 ABCA 19, Justice Veldhuis said: 4 Rules 14.37(2) and 14.58 of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, gives authority to a single appeal judge to grant leave to a party to intervene in an appeal and impose conditions on the intervention.
The intervener cannot raise or argue novel issues on appeal: Rule 14.58(3).
5 Intervener status will be granted where the applicant:
(1) is directly and significantly affected by the outcome of the appeal, and
(2) has expertise and a fresh perspective on the subject matter of the appeal that is useful for the appeal's resolution: R v Morgentaler, [1993] 1 SCR 462 at para 1, [1993] SCJ No 48 (QL)
City of Edmonton v Edmonton (Subdivision and Development Appeal Board), 2014 ABCA 340 at para 8, 584 AR 255.
The factors that inform these two questions include (Pedersen v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 192 at para 3, 432 AR 219; Re Stewart Estate, 2014 ABCA 222 at para 5, 577 AR 57): 1.
Will the intervener be directly affected by the appeal; 2.
Is the presence of the intervener necessary for the Court to properly decide the matter; 3.
Might the intervener's interest in the proceedings not be fully protected by the parties; 4.
Will the intervener's submission be useful and different or bring particular expertise to the subject matter of the appeal; 5.
Will the intervention unduly delay the proceedings; 6.
Will there possibly be prejudice to the parties if intervention is granted; 7.
Will intervention widen the lis between the parties; and 8.
Will the intervention transform the Court into a political arena?

6 The discretion to grant intervener status should be exercised sparingly, particularly in criminal proceedings where the dispute must remain between the accused and the Crown: R v Neve, [1996] 8 WWR 294 at para 16, 184 AR 359 (CA).

Interventions in criminal appeals are “generally shunned by the courts for a variety of policy and prudential reasons”, especially the risk “that the hearing of other voices can distort an appeal”: R v JLA, 2009 ABCA 324 at para 2, 464 AR 310.
In Orphan Well Assn. v.
Grant Thorton Ltd., 2016 ABCA 238, 2016 CarswellAlta 1466, see annotation under 1.
Intervenor Status.
See also: Styles v.
Alberta Investment Management Corp., 2016 ABCA 218, 2016 CarswellAlta 1371 at paragraphs 13–15.
See also: Canadian Centre for Bio-Ethical Reform v.
Grande Prairie (City), 2017 ABCA 280, 2017 CarswellAlta 1571 at paragraphs 8–11.
In AC and JF v.

Alberta, 2020 ABCA 309, 2020 CarswellAlta 1571, the Court said: [8] Under Rules 14.37(2)(e) and 14.58 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, a single appeal judge has authority to grant permission to intervene in an appeal and to impose conditions on the intervention.
[9] All parties to these applications agree on the test for permission to intervene.
I must consider
(1) whether the proposed intervenor has a particular interest in, or will be directly and significantly affected by the outcome of the appeal, or
(2) whether the intervenor will provide some special expertise, perspective, or information that will help resolve the appeal: Edmonton (City) v Urban Development Institute, 2014 ABCA 340 at para 8
Hamm v Canada (Attorney General), 2019 ABCA 389 at para 5
Papaschase Indian Band No 136 v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320 at para 5 [Papaschase].
[10] Other relevant considerations include: 1.
Is the presence of the intervenor necessary for the court to properly decide the matter?
Might the intervenor's interest in the proceedings not be fully protected by the parties?
Will the intervention unduly delay the proceedings?
Will there be possible prejudice to the parties if intervention is granted?
Will intervention widen the dispute between the parties?
Will the intervention transform the court into a political arena?
Will the intervener's submission be useful and different or bring particular expertise to the subject matter of the appeal?
UAlberta Pro-Life v Governors of the University of Alberta, 2018 ABCA 350 at para 10; Pederson v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 192 at para 3.
[11] With respect to the scope of intervenor submissions, the case law establishes there are no bright lines precluding an intervenor from raising issues and argument not raised below.

If the proposed new issues or arguments require fresh evidence or prejudice a party, they are likely impermissible: Papaschase at para 3 citing Batchewana Indian Band v Canada (Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs (1996), 199 NR 1.

Even absent the need for fresh evidence or possible prejudice, it is not “appropriate for an intervener to extend legal argument well beyond what the courts below and the parties have advanced”: Deloitte & Touche v Ontario, 2003 SCC 61 at para 31.
Courts should be guided by the causes of action in the pleadings.

So, for example, an intervenor should not be permitted to raise constitutional issues where no constitutional issues have been raised in the pleadings: Johnston v Alberta (Vital Statistics), 2008 ABCA 2 at para 7.
However, arguing a new point inextricably linked to an issue the parties have already put before the court is permissible.

An example of this is found in Alberta (Minister of Justice) v Métis Settlements Appeal Tribunal, 2005 ABCA 143, at para 9, where the intervenor was permitted to argue the potential application of s 25 of the Charter as it was inextricably linked to other sections of the Charter already in issue.

[12] The Supreme Court of Canada said at para 40 of Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada (Minister of Canadian Heritage), 2005 SCC 69 that “an intervenor is in no worse a position than a party who belatedly discovers some legal argument that it ought to have raised earlier in the proceedings but did not.” An intervenor may always “put forward any legal argument in support of what it submits is the correct legal conclusion on an issue properly before the Court, provided that in doing so its legal argument does not require additional facts”: Mikisew at para 40.
In Wesley v.

Alberta, 2023 ABCA 289, the Court of Appeal noted that the factors of “particular interest in the outcome of the appeal” and “special expertise” do not create an “either/or” situation; both factors should be considered in an application for intervenor status.
At paragraph 8, the Court said: [8] More recently, in VLM v Dominey Estate, 2023 ABCA 226, Slatter JA noted that the test for intervention “is based on
(1) whether the proposed intervenor has a particular interest in, or will be directly and significantly affected by the outcome of the appeal, or
(2) whether the intervenor will provide some special expertise, perspective, or information that will help resolve the appeal”: para 2.
An intervenor “does not have to satisfy both branches of the test… intervenor status does not automatically follow from showing either an ‘interest’ or a ‘fresh perspective’.
The test is not strictly conjunctive or disjunctive, but rather involves a consideration of both factors in all cases”: para 3.
Applications to Intervene on an Application to Seek Leave to Appeal In Balancing Pool v.

ENMAX Energy Corporation, 2018 ABCA 143, 2018 CarswellAlta 698, the Alberta Utilities Commission issued a ruling after a hearing, and some of the parties (“predecessor STS contract holders”) in that hearing applied for leave to appeal the AUC's decision to the Court of Appeal.

Balancing Pool (and others) applied to Justice Paperny for an order adding them as parties or, alternatively, intervenors, to the application for leave to appeal made by the predecessor STS contract holders.
In ruling on the application, Justice Paperny discussed applications to add parties or intervenors to applications for leave to appeal.

Her Ladyship said: 20 This Court has an inherent power to add parties to an appeal should it find that it is in the interests of justice to do so: Hayes v Mayhood et al, [1959] SCR 568, 18 DLR (2d) 497.
The guiding principles have been set forth in Carbon Development Partnership v Alberta (Energy and Utilities Board), 2007 ABCA 231, [2007] A.J.
No.

727 (QL) at para 9: This court has inherent power to add parties to an appeal, especially if an applicant's interests are not represented: … The joinder test is whether or not the applicant has a legal interest in the outcome of the proceeding.
If so, there are two different sub-tests.
The first is whether it is just and convenient to add the applicant.
The second is whether or not the applicant's interest would only be adequately protected if it were granted party status.
21 However, this Court strongly discourages adding parties or allowing intervenors at this earlier stage, for the purpose of an application for permission to appeal.

The reason for this is clear: in the absence of permission to appeal being granted, there is no appeal and as such no interest, legal or economic, that can be directly affected by the application (at least immediately).
If the application to appeal is granted, parties are at liberty to apply for status at the hearing of the appeal.
If the application is dismissed, there is no appeal.
Unless and until permission is granted, proposed parties are not generally at risk.
Usually the issues on a permission application are narrow and are focussed on the statutory requirements.
In other words, the inquiry at that stage is usually a narrow one and rarely assisted by representations from multiple parties.
22 For these reasons, this Court has held that adding parties or intervenors should be discouraged at this stage of the proceedings absent extraordinary circumstances.
As stated by Hunt JA in Carbon at para 6: Applications for intervener status in leave applications are rare.
In the Board context, leave to appeal can only be granted if important questions of law or jurisdiction are raised: Alberta Energy and Utilities Board Act, R.S.A.
26(1) (“AEUB Act”).
At this stage, it is unknown whether leave will be granted and, if so, on what questions.
It is therefore extremely difficult to know what interests, if any, of the applicants may be affected and what, if anything, they may be able to contribute to the proceedings.

This no doubt explains the wisdom behind the Supreme Court of Canada's practice to usually defer intervener applications until after leave has been granted, even if a party has enjoyed intervener status before the lower courts: R. v.
857 at para.
An even stronger rational for awaiting the outcome of the leave applications may exist in regulatory proceedings like this where, if leave is granted, the questions will be limited in scope.
Costs In Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association Inc. v.
Thomson, 2024 ABCA 43, the Association unsuccessfully sought intervenor status in an appeal dealing with the interpretation of a life insurance policy.
The question arose: should the Association pay costs to the party which successfully opposed the application for intervenor status?
Justice Pentelechuk discussed when costs might be awarded against intervenors (or those seeking intervenor status), and awarded costs against the Association.
Her Ladyship said: [2] Indeed, the general rule that costs are neither awarded to nor against interveners is longstanding: see Harper v Harper, 1979 CanLII 168 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 2 at 16
Young v Young, 1993 CanLII 34 (SCC), [1993] 4 SCR 3 at 138; and B(R) v Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto, 1995 CanLII 115 (SCC), [1995] 1 SCR 315.
B(R) was a case where the intervener in question was the Ontario Attorney General.

The court was explicit about the rule relating to a “public intervener”, referring to an award of “costs against an intervening Attorney General, acting… in the public interest” being permitted “only in very rare cases” (para 122), “the rule that a party granted intervener status in the public interest is, generally, neither entitled to nor liable for the costs in the matter” (para 176) and “the general rule that costs not be awarded to or against an intervener in the public interest” (para 178).
[3] It is clear from review of the case law that the court's discretion to award costs both to and against an intervener is not fettered by this general rule.

[4] In Alberta, while this Court has acknowledged the general rule that an intervener should bear its own costs, it does not necessarily follow from such a general rule that an intervener should never be liable for costs.

For instance, Slatter JA in Métis Nation of Alberta Association v Alberta (Indigenous Relations), 2022 ABCA 250 at para 17 held that while those granted intervener status are not entitled to costs of the appeal or the intervener applications, “[w]hether they are liable to pay costs will be in the discretion of the panel that hears the appeal” [emphasis added].

In Armcorp 4-18 Ltd (Bankruptcy of the Estates) v Canada, 1999 ABCA 95 at para 15, after dismissing the appeal this Court ordered the intervener, the Royal Bank of Canada, to pay costs of an intervention motion.
[5] Historically, the general rule regarding costs has been tied to “public interest” interventions, often involving constitutional challenges.
There are sound policy reasons for doing so, rooted in notions of access to justice and advocacy in matters of public importance.
But many interventions seek to advance private interests.
[6] The distinction between public and private interveners was explored in Incredible Electronics Inc v Canada (Attorney General) (2006), 2006 CanLII 17939 (ON SC), 80 OR (3d) 723 (SC).

In Perell J's view, classifying the intervener's involvement as either public or private interest helps determine whether the intervener falls within or outside the normal rule that interveners neither receive nor pay costs.
[7] I agree with this reasoning.
Admittedly, there are no bright lines separating public interest interveners from those advancing private interests.
Public interest interveners can have private interests also furthered by the intervention….
[8] Classifying the intervention as, or predominantly as, public interest or private interest is an important consideration in determining whether the general rule on costs should apply.
Intervention applications are increasingly common.

Some are successful, some are not, but when the interest advanced is a private one and the application is unsuccessful, there is no principled reason why the proposed intervener should not bear costs.
Awarding costs in the appropriate case may also serve to mitigate against interventions that are nothing but “busybody” applications: see Wong v Giannacopoulos, 2011 ABCA 206 at para 10. ….
[10] The Association is not a public interest litigant, rather it represents the majority of life insurers in Canada.
The Association's proposed application was clearly made to further private interests.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.59:1 Rule 14.59 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.59. 1. An Offer in relation to the appeal is necessary In 864503 Alberta Inc. v. Genco Place Properties Ltd., 2019 ABCA 248, 2019 CarswellAlta 1161, the successful party to an appeal (Genco) sought double costs in the Court of Appeal on the basis of an offer made in the proceedings while the matter was still before the Court of Queen's Bench. While the Court awarded double costs in relation to the steps taken in the Court of Queen's Bench, the Court did not order double costs in the Court of Appeal. The Court said: [19] … We conclude, therefore, that Genco is entitled to double costs in the Court of Queen's Bench from the date of the formal offer. [20] The same is not true of proceedings on appeal to this court, however. Rule 14.59 contemplates a doubling of costs relating to an appeal where “a formal offer to settle the appeal or any part of the appeal” is made. No formal offer was made in relation to the appeal. Genco points to a decision of this court in which costs of an appeal were doubled based on a pretrial formal offer, even though the offer was not renewed prior to appeal: 321665 Alberta Ltd v Husky Oil Operations Ltd., 2013 ABCA 326 (CanLII) at paras 32-33. However, that case was decided before the Court of Appeal Rules were amended to include the current r 14.59. In a case decided under the current rules, appeal costs were not doubled where there was no renewal of the offer, or further offer, in the Court of Appeal: Humphreys v Trebilcock, 2017 ABCA 232 (CanLII) at paras 4-5. See also Alberta v Nilsson, 2003 ABCA 134 (CanLII) at paras 15–21 In Bruen v. University of Calgary, 2019 ABCA 275, 2019 CarswellAlta 1390, the Court said: [7] Rule 14.59 provides for the doubling of costs when a formal offer to settle an appeal is made, and the party making the offer achieves greater success on the appeal. Informal offers, such as Calderbank offers, are also relevant to costs, although doubling is not automatic or presumed: Koma v Tomich Estate, 2011 ABCA 257 (CanLII) at para. 6, 70 ETR (3d) 1. Where informal offers are involved, the court has a wide discretion over costs, and there is no “one-size fits all” response to nominal offers to settle: Carroll at para. 3. [8] The costs rules respecting offers are designed to encourage the principled and reasonable settlement of litigation, and to deter litigants from taking unreasonable positions. In order to attract costs consequences, offers must be realistic, reasonable and represent a bona fide compromise or other articulable reason for settlement: Allen (Next Friend of) v University Hospitals Board, 2006 ABCA 101 (CanLII) at paras. 12–5, 59 Alta LR (4th) 1, 384 AR 23. They are not to be used as a mere stratagem for doubling costs: Allen (Next Friend) at para. 16. The courts view with scepticism offers to merely abandon actions or appeals, or to do so for nominal sums. An offer to the other party that they “think again” generally contains no element of compromise, and is unlikely to promote settlement. 2. Double costs In H2S Solutions Ltd v. Tourmaline Oil Corp, 2020 ABCA 201, 2020 CarswellAlta 926, 7 Alta. L.R. (7th) 232, the Court said that its decision in that case was “the opportunity to simplify and clarify the factors relevant to the Court for a principled application of the double costs rule on appeal.” The Court said: [27] The double costs rules are aimed at encouraging timely and efficient resolution of disputes, and preventing needless appeals. The rules encourage parties to resolve matters by offering identifiable and sufficient compromises to settle litigation, and to subject litigants who reject identifiable and sufficient compromises to predictable, more severe costs consequences. [28] The primary factors bearing upon the question whether the double costs rule (a) has been triggered and (b) if so, ought to be applied, are the following, recognizing they do not represent a closed list. i) — timing of the offer [29] In some circumstances, the timing of the offer is an important consideration. [30] Pursuant to Schedule C, item 19(1), typically a respondent does not incur tariff appeal costs until its factum preparation is underway. But, if an offer is made before a respondent incurs costs but does not expire until after costs have been incurred, there is no principled basis for this Court to refuse awarding double costs to the successful offeror for all claimable tariff items. The reason for this is that the offeree had the option of accepting the offer before any costs were incurred by the offeror, but did not. What began as an offer revealing no identifiable and sufficient compromise becomes, over the course of its currency, a genuine offer of compromise to forego costs accumulated. [31] Further, the rules provide for acceptance of an offer “until the earlier of the expiry of 2 months after the date of the offer or any longer period specified in the offer, and the start of the oral hearing of the appeal”; accordingly, the discrete specifics of what costs accumulated during the currency of the unaccepted offer is often an important factor. [32] Of course, in addition to timing, the content of the offer must be considered. ii) — content of the offer [33] Presenting something that amounts to a no-risk, “think again” tactic where the offeror, in effect, is offering nothing does not trigger the double costs rules because it contains no identifiable and sufficient compromise. In essence, not qualifying as an offer, it does not trigger the mandatory doubling effect of the rules. iii) — beyond de minimus [34] An identifiable offer is one that is beyond de minimus. For example, an offer to pay $1.00, without more, is de minimus. But, an offer to forego a previous award of costs, or to agree to settle part of the outstanding litigation, or to discount an extant judgment, would be identifiable and sufficient compromises. The content of offers that would trigger the double costs rules is limited only by the imagination of litigants. [35] To be clear, however, nothing more will be required to trigger the double costs rules than that the Court is able to readily identify the element(s) of compromise contained in a pre-hearing offer, and nothing more will be needed for the double costs rules to be applied, subject only to “special circumstances”, discussed below. [36] This Court will not engage in a hindsight assessment of the relative merits of the live issues, as this type of exercise squanders finite judicial resources. This Court will not entertain protests that the double costs rules ought not to apply because the offer was only made for “tactical” advantage (whatever that actually means). Nor will this Court undertake a search for the elusive compromise that is not immediately obvious. It is up to the offeror, not the Court, to ensure that the offer it makes is plain on its face as to what the offeror is prepared to give up, in exchange for concluding the appeal by way of a discontinuance. [37] To conclude, provided the offer is made no later than 10 days before the appeal is scheduled to be heard, and is not withdrawn, and provided it contains an identifiable and sufficient compromise, the double costs rule will apply to all tariff appeal steps claimable by the offeror. [38] This conclusion is subject only to the operation of the rule relating to “special circumstances”. [39] This Court possesses a residual and overarching discretion to disallow double costs in certain circumstances, even where the rules are triggered, by reason of “special circumstances”: rule 4.29(4)(e). Rule 4.29(4)(e) is an exception, to be employed by the Court where double costs are not justified despite the offeror having made an offer that otherwise would trigger the rules; see, for example, see for example, Stevenson & Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook, vol 1 (Edmonton: Juriliber 2019) at 4–54 to 4–55.

[32] Of course, in addition to timing, the content of the offer must be considered. ii) — content of the offer [33] Presenting something that amounts to a no-risk, “think again” tactic where the offeror, in effect, is offering nothing does not trigger the double costs rules because it contains no identifiable and sufficient compromise.
In essence, not qualifying as an offer, it does not trigger the mandatory doubling effect of the rules. iii) — beyond de minimus [34] An identifiable offer is one that is beyond de minimus.
For example, an offer to pay $1.00, without more, is de minimus.
But, an offer to forego a previous award of costs, or to agree to settle part of the outstanding litigation, or to discount an extant judgment, would be identifiable and sufficient compromises.
The content of offers that would trigger the double costs rules is limited only by the imagination of litigants.

[35] To be clear, however, nothing more will be required to trigger the double costs rules than that the Court is able to readily identify the element(s) of compromise contained in a pre-hearing offer, and nothing more will be needed for the double costs rules to be applied, subject only to “special circumstances”, discussed below.
[36] This Court will not engage in a hindsight assessment of the relative merits of the live issues, as this type of exercise squanders finite judicial resources.
This Court will not entertain protests that the double costs rules ought not to apply because the offer was only made for “tactical” advantage (whatever that actually means).
Nor will this Court undertake a search for the elusive compromise that is not immediately obvious.

It is up to the offeror, not the Court, to ensure that the offer it makes is plain on its face as to what the offeror is prepared to give up, in exchange for concluding the appeal by way of a discontinuance.

[37] To conclude, provided the offer is made no later than 10 days before the appeal is scheduled to be heard, and is not withdrawn, and provided it contains an identifiable and sufficient compromise, the double costs rule will apply to all tariff appeal steps claimable by the offeror.
[38] This conclusion is subject only to the operation of the rule relating to “special circumstances”.

[39] This Court possesses a residual and overarching discretion to disallow double costs in certain circumstances, even where the rules are triggered, by reason of “special circumstances”: rule 4.29(4)(e).

Rule 4.29(4)(e) is an exception, to be employed by the Court where double costs are not justified despite the offeror having made an offer that otherwise would trigger the rules; see, for example, see for example, Stevenson & Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook, vol 1 (Edmonton: Juriliber 2019) at 4–54 to 4–55.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.64:1 Rule 14.64 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.64. 1. Three Categories of Deadlines In Li v. Morgan, 2020 ABCA 186, 2020 CarswellAlta 846, 8 Alta. L.R. (7th) 65, Justice Statter gave the following overview of the types of deadlines which affect appeals: [3] Appeals must be commenced and completed within a number of different deadlines. The three main categories of deadline are: a) The deadline to start the appeal; b) Deadlines to take various steps needed to prepare the appeal for oral argument; and c) The six month deadline to restore an appeal that has been struck for failure to meet one of the deadlines mentioned in clause b). While the tests in the three categories overlap, there are important differences. Cases in one category do not necessarily apply to the others. [4] Deadlines for starting an appeal are short, because of the importance of finality in litigation. The successful party is entitled to know promptly if the judgment is being challenged by appeal. The test for extending the time to appeal is set out in a long line of cases, tracing back to Cairns v Cairns, 1931 CanLII 471 (AB CA), [1931] 4 DLR 819 at pp. 826–7 (Alta SC AD). The traditional test is summarized in cases like Lofstrom v Radke, 2017 ABCA 211 at para. 3, 56 Alta LR (6th) 52: a) a bona fide intention to appeal while the right to appeal existed; b) an explanation for the failure to appeal in time that serves to excuse or justify the lateness; c) an absence of serious prejudice such that it would not be unjust to disturb the judgment; d) the applicant must not have taken the benefits of the judgment under appeal; and e) a reasonable chance of success on the appeal, which might better be described as a reasonably arguable appeal. These factors guide the Court in exercising its overriding general discretion to extend the time to appeal. It is not necessary for an applicant to satisfy all components of the test, and they do not set rigid requirements. [5] Once an appeal is launched, the successful party knows that the judgment is being challenged. The Rules of Court then impose a number of deadlines for the steps that must be taken to prepare the case for oral argument. The objective at this stage is to avoid delay. Some deadlines for fast track appeals are shorter than those for standard appeals. Some rules provide that the appeal will be struck if the deadline is missed: R. 14.16(3): filing the Appeal Record; R. 14.23(1) and 14.24(1): filing the appellant's factum. The delay in these cases can sometimes be as short as a day or two. [6] Applications to restore appeals struck under these rules are governed by the following test: a) An explanation for the delay that caused the appeal to be struck; b) Reasonable promptness in moving to cure the defect and have the appeal restored; c) Continuing intention to proceed with the appeal; d) Lack of prejudice to the respondent (including the length of the delay); and e) The arguable merit of the appeal. See for example, EXP Mining Equipment Rentals Inc v Caterpillar Financial Services Ltd., 2017 ABCA 364 at para. 19 and Prochazka v Alberta (Maintenance Enforcement Program), 2014 ABCA 448 at para 4. No one factor is determinative. All factors are weighed to determine whether it is in the interests of justice for the appeal to be restored. [7] The third category is the deadline to restore an appeal that has been struck. This is governed by R. 14.47 and 14.65(3). These rules confirm that an application to restore a standard appeal that has been struck, dismissed or deemed abandoned must be filed, returnable and granted within six months of it having been struck, dismissed or deemed abandoned. These rules have an administrative component, because after the six months has passed the Registry can regard the appeal as “finished”, and the file can be closed and archived. However, the passage of the six month time limit is also a line-in-the-sand in terms of the test for restoring the appeal. [8] The test to restore an appeal after the six month deemed abandonment deadline includes the following considerations: a. An explanation for the delay that caused the appeal to be struck in the first place; b. An explanation for the delay in applying to restore the appeal; c. Continuing intention to proceed with the appeal; d. Lack of prejudice to the respondent; e. The arguable merit of the appeal. Again, no one factor is determinative. All factors are weighed to determine whether it is in the interests of justice for the appeal to be restored. [9] Once the six month line-in-the-sand deadline has passed, the components of the test are stricter: Allen v Alberta (Seniors and Community Supports), 2015 ABCA 238 at para 5. Appeals are to be diligently prosecuted, and when an appeal has been struck for six months, prejudice to the respondent can be assumed. As noted, at some point the successful party has a legitimate expectation that the judgment is final. Nevertheless, while the test is stricter at this stage, requiring “no control” and “impossibility”, as suggested in Scarlett v Wang, 2019 ABCA 72 at para 29, runs the risk of establishing a test that is impossible to meet. [10] The Court has a discretion under R. 13.5(2) and 14.2(3) to extend most deadlines, including the six month deadline in R. 14.47 and 14.65(3). When a deadline cannot be met, the proper approach is to apply for an extension before the deadline passes. The Case Management Officers deal with most such requests under R. 14.36. However, when a deadline is missed, relief is still available. 2. Difference between Striking and Dismissing an Appeal In Dallaire v. Ducap (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 321 (C.A.), Berger J.A. noted the differences between striking an appeal from the appeal list [R. 14.64], and dismissing an appeal for want of prosecution [Rules 14.62 and 14.63]. At p. 322, His Lordship said: Rule 516 makes clear that a single Judge of the Court of Appeal may make any Order in chambers in respect of any matter incidental to [an] appeal. Rule 515.1(7) allows an appeal to be struck by the presiding Judge when the general appeal list is spoken to. But a Motion to dismiss is not a Motion to strike. If an appeal is struck, the Appellant may apply to restore the case to the list. On the other hand, if an appeal is dismissed, the remedy from such a final adjudication is an application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.

sentences.text: Restoring appeals

paragraphs.text: (1) An appeal or application for permission to appeal that has been struck by operation of these rules or the provisions of any order, or by failure of any party to appear when required, may be restored (a) with the filed written consent of the parties or by order of a single appeal judge on application under rule 14.47, and (b) on the payment of the fee for an application to restore an appeal in Schedule B. (3) An appeal or application is deemed to have been abandoned if no application to restore an appeal or application for permission to appeal has been filed, served and granted (a) for a standard appeal, within 6 months after having been struck, dismissed or deemed abandoned, and (b) for a fast track appeal, within 3 months after having been struck, dismissed or deemed abandoned.
