paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.65:1 Rule 14.65 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.65. 1. Discretion to Restore In Taylor v. 1103919 Alberta Ltd., 2015 ABCA 201, the Court said: 21 Restoration of an appeal struck for failure to comply with the filing requirements of the Rules of Court engages the following considerations: a) arguable merit to the appeal; b) explanation for the defect or delay which caused the appeal to be taken off the list; c) reasonable promptness in moving to cure the defect and have the appeal restored to the list; d) intention in time to proceed with the appeal; and e) lack of prejudice to the respondents (including length of delay) See Prochazka v Alberta (Maintenance Enforcement Program), 2014 ABCA 448 at para 4; Gould v Gould, 2014 ABCA 144 at para 4; Garry v Canada, 2007 ABCA 234 at para 4, 429 AR 292; 707739 Alberta v Phillips, 2001 ABCA 219 at para 13, 286 AR 367. In Kent v. MacDonald, 2020 ABCA 91, 2020 CarswellAlta 379, Justice Feehan said: [11] The first factor, arguable merit, in the context of an application to restore an appeal is a very low bar: all the applicants must establish is that their appeal is not hopeless or frivolous: Murphy v Haworth, 2016 ABCA 219, para 23, 2 CPC (8th) 201; Condominium Plan No 982 6403 v CPI Crown Properties International Corporation, 2018 ABCA 232, para 16, 76 Alta LR (6th) 318. The onus is on the applicants to show the appeals are not bound to fail: 932282 Alberta Ltd v Royal Bank of Canada, 2019 ABCA 252, paras 18–19. [12] None of the factors the Court considers is determinative; the failure of the applicant to meet one of the factors is not fatal, because all of the factors are weighed to determine, whether, overall, it is in the interests of justice to restore the appeal and allow the matter to proceed: Prochazka, para 4; Mylonas, para 4; Clark v Institute of Chartered Accountants of Alberta (Complaints Inquiry Committee), 2015 ABCA 271, para 5, 607 AR 1; Templanza v Ford, 2019 ABCA 309, para 20. In R. v. Alam, 2020 ABCA 10, 2020 CarswellAlta 22, Justice Rowbotham had before her an application to restore a conviction appeal. Her Ladyship said: [8] The threshold for restoring an appeal is heightened when the appeal is deemed abandoned: see Clark v Institute of Chartered Accountants of Alberta (Complaints Inquiry Committee), 2015 ABCA 271 at para 6; Allen v Alberta (Seniors and Community Supports), 2015 ABCA 238 at para 5; and Scarlett v Wang, 2019 ABCA 72 at paras 25–30. It has been said that the discretion to restore an appeal ought to be exercised sparingly: Allen at para 5. The same test applies in a criminal appeal: R v Reeves, 2004 ABCA 376; R v Foulston, 1994 ABCA 362; R v McMahon, 2018 ABCA 344; R v Mian, 2012 ABCA 15. In 422252 Alberta Ltd. v. Messenger, 2015 ABCA 47, Justice Berger said: 4 This Court has repeatedly made clear that the decision on whether to restore an appeal involves an exercise of discretion. Several factors must be taken into account. All must be weighed to determine whether the interests of justice warrant that the appeal proceed: • The reason why the appeal was struck. • The length of the delay in bringing the application to restore. • The overall conduct of the litigation. • Prejudice to the Respondent. • The merits of the appeal. See Morbank Financial Inc. v. Field, 2014 ABCA 3, Can-Cell Industries Inc. v. Lippa, 2010 ABCA 409, Ruskin Estate v. Chutskoff Estate, 2013 ABCA 276. In Phillips v. 707739 Alberta Ltd. (2001), 286 A.R. 367 (C.A. [In Chambers]); leave to appeal refused 2002 CarswellAlta 864, 2002 CarswellAlta 865 (S.C.C.), Hunt J.A. considered the discretion to be exercised under Rule 14.65. At p. 371, Her Ladyship said: An order to restore an appeal under Rule 515.1(7) is discretionary and, in exercising that discretion, a judge must consider all relevant matters. … A mere slip or inadvertence to appear on the part of counsel will generally not prevent the restoration of the appeal to the list. … On the other hand, panels of this court have refused applications to restore struck appeals on a number of grounds: an appeal appears to lack merit …; an appellant show no intention of proceeding with an appeal and has not taken any steps to prosecute his appeal with diligence …; the delay is so great that prejudice to the respondents is evident …; and an appellant can offer no reasonable explanation for a lengthy delay in taking steps to restore an appeal. … In Kieser v. Kieser (2003), 327 A.R. 390 (C.A.) referred to the above quote with approval, and said, at p. 392: In this case, counsel for Mr. Kieser has confined his opposition to the restoration of the matter to the list on the basis that the appeal appears to lack merit. In my view, the onus is on the party who is asserting that the appeal appears to lack merit to establish that it appears to be without merit. However, in Walsh v. Chotalia, 2015 ABCA 244, Justice Côté cast doubt on the decision in Kieser. At paragraphs 9–10 of Walsh, his Lordship said: 9 One early authority briefly suggested that the onus is on the respondent to show that the appeal has no merit: Kieser v Kieser, 2003 ABCA 152, 327 AR 390 (one JA) (para 6). It offers no authority or discussion. That would require the respondents to disprove a negative, virtually beyond a reasonable doubt. Maybe even require them to read the appellant's mind. The appellant could remain mute. After all, a civil notice of appeal does not require that grounds of appeal be stated. 10 In 2003 there had been few decisions on restoring appeals. Since then, dozens have been decided, and lack of merit is the most common ground to refuse to restore. Justices constantly rely upon the fact that the appellant has not enunciated an arguable ground of appeal. Many other cases put the onus of showing arguable merit on the applicant (which is the usual rule on any application). See for example Knight v Director of Child etc, 2012 ABCA 377, 542 AR 22 (paras 17–23) (one JA). Many reported cases implicitly require the applicant appellant to show arguable merit. Of course the degree of proof of arguable merits is a lax test. In most cases, who has the onus does not matter much, as some evidence or argument is present. In Winners Equities Inc. v. 664050 Alberta Ltd. (2006), 401 A.R. 94 (Alta. C.A.), Côté J.A. said, at p. 96: 9 According to the case law, the court must weigh the extent of, and reasons for, the delay or violation of the Rules or Practice Directions, to decide whether to restore the appeal to the list: Craig v. Craig, [2004] A.J. No. 1280, 2004 ABCA 365, [2005] A.R. Uned. 388, Calg. 0201-0094-AC (one J.A. Nov. 16). That includes delay after the striking off: R. v. Reeves, [2004] A.J. No. 1305, 2004 ABCA 376, [2004] A.R. Uned. 506, Calg. 01-02275 (one J.A. Nov. 23); Wingrove v. Wingrove, [2005] A.J. No. 452, 2005 ABCA 149, [2005] A.R. Uned. 57, Edm. 0303-0176-AC (one J.A. Apr. 21). Though these authorities for that precise point are all unreported, the law on other types of opening up default is to the same effect.… His Lordship then said, at p. 96: 12 It is now fashionable to separate a party from his or her lawyer when questions of neglect or delay arise in civil procedure; many cases recognize that tacitly. However, in my respectful view, it is not enough to swear merely that one hired a lawyer, and did not know that he was doing nothing. In Neumann v. Alberta (Human Rights & Citizenship Commission) (2006), 401 A.R. 165 (Alta. C.A.), Ritter J.A. said at p. 166: 3 When considering whether an appeal should be restored, several factors are relevant including the length of delay, the explanation for the delay, and the prejudice (if any) to both the respondents and the appellant: Winners Equities Inc. v. 664050 Alberta Ltd., [2006] A.J. No. 1580, 2006 ABCA 394. The merits of the appeal and the diligence in prosecuting the appeal are also relevant factors: Arabian Muslim Association v. Canadian Islamic Centre, [2005] A.J. No. 1160, 2005 ABCA 288, at para. 3. In Carbone v. Whidden, 2013 ABCA 346, 2013 CarswellAlta 1950, 561 A.R. 158, the applicant sought restoration to the appeal list of her appeal of several orders made by the case management judge appointed to manage the trial of Ms. Carbone's medical malpractice claim. Justice Conrad said, at paragraphs 14–16: 14 The only question is whether I should exercise my discretion to restore the appeal. A justice of the Court of Appeal possesses a broad discretion to restore an appeal to the appellate list. In exercising that discretion the court examines such factors as the reasons for the delay, any prejudice that may arise, as well as the relative merits of the appeal. I also find that in appeals such as this, where the appeal is from a pre-trial order which does not end the trial, a judge should also look at the nature of the appeal and consider the effect of a successful appeal on the trial of the case as a whole. 15 Further, where an appeal is subject to the Part J appeal procedures of the CPD, the importance of early disposition should be considered and placed on the scale of factors. The procedures for Part J appeals are aimed at expediting trials. 16 As noted, the decision to restore is highly discretionary; 707739 Alberta Ltd v. Phillips, 2001 ABCA 219, 286 AR 367 is an authority requiring only “a limited consideration of the merits of the appeal” and it has been suggested that an applicant need only show that her appeal is “reasonably arguable”: see Muhtady v. Sarhan, 2013 ABCA 197 at para 6, (available on line). Madam Justice Conrad made the following comments about assessing the merits of the appeal (at paragraphs 21–22): 21 Finally, I turn to the merits of this appeal. I accept that the merits need not meet a high standard. Nevertheless, it is important to address this issue. When addressing the issue of merit, it is important to view the arguments through the proper standard of review. The applicant argues that all of the case management judge's orders must be viewed on the standard of correctness. The respondent argues that they are discretionary orders and therefore reasonableness is the appropriate standard. 22 In my view, there is no one standard for decisions of a case management judge—the standard depends upon the issue involved. For example, while interpretation of the Rules of Court may be reviewed for correctness, orders relating to the nature and scope of questioning fall within a judge's discretion and are entitled to considerable deference: see Golden Estate v. Neilson, 2011 ABCA 338 at para 12, 519 AR 165. 2. Restoration of an Appeal To The General Appeal List In Koerner v. Capital Health Authority, 2011 ABCA 131, 2011 CarswellAlta 688, 515 A.R. 385, 6 C.P.C. (7th) 229, 532 W.A.C. 385, Justice Berger said, at paragraphs 10-11: 10 The conditions precedent to restore an appeal that has been struck are the following: 1. The Court retains the discretion to restore the appeal: 707739 Alberta Ltd. v. Phillips, 2001 ABCA 219, 286 A.R. 367, leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused [2002] S.C.C.A. No. 64. 2. In deciding whether to restore an appeal that has been deemed abandoned, the court will consider such matters as the timely intention to appeal, inordinate delay, explanations or excuses for the delay, prejudice to the respondents, and whether it is in the interests of justice that the appeal be reinstated: Phillips at para.14. 3. The case law, summarized at para. 13 of Phillips indicates: … An order to restore an appeal struck from the list under Rule 515.1(7) is discretionary and, in exercising that discretion, a judge must consider all relevant matters: Brown v. Royal Bank of Canada (2001), 277 A.R. 241 at 242 (C.A.). A mere slip or inadvertence to appear on the part of counsel will generally not prevent the restoration of the appeal to the list: ibid.; Bishop v. Bishop (1990), 113 A.R. 280 (C.A.). On the other hand, panels of this Court have refused applications to restore struck appeals on a number of grounds: an appeal appears to lack merit: Kowalchuk v. Kowalchuk, [1999] A.J. No. 1585; … an appellant shows no intention of proceeding with an appeal and has not taken any steps to prosecute his appeal with diligence: Sammut v. Landau Estate, [1989] A.J. No. 128; … the delay is so great that prejudice to the respondents is evident: Clay v. Board of Reference and Board of Education (1990), 106 A.R. 24; and an appellant can offer no reasonable explanation for a lengthy delay in taking steps to restore and appeal: Kalin v. Cline, [1992] A.J. No. 893. … 11 Phillips was applied in Tinant v. Tinant, 2003 ABCA 211, 330 A.R. 148 (single J.A.), where an application to restore an appeal to the list was denied because of inordinate delay and an inadequate explanation. See also Chase v. Chase, 2003 ABCA 29, 320 A.R. 201, Petersen v. Paplinski, 2004 ABCA 58 and Craig v. Craig, 2004 ABCA 365. See also: Dahmer v. Dahmer, 2012 ABCA 120, 2012 CarswellAlta 688 in which Berger, J.A. reiterated the law set out above (see paragraph 1). In Cameron Corp. v. Edmonton (Subdivision and Development Appeal Board), 2012 ABCA 256, 2012 CarswellAlta 1476, 536 A.R. 171, Justice Slatter said, at paragraph 6: 6 Deciding whether to restore an appeal that has been struck involves a consideration of all relevant factors: Dahlseide v. Dahlseide, 2010 ABCA 220 at para. 10; 707739 Alberta Ltd. v. Phillips, 2001 ABCA 219 at para. 13, 286 AR 367 leave to appeal refused [2002] S.C.C.A. No. 64, [2002] 2 SCR v. The following factors are often considered: (a) whether there was a continuing intention to prosecute the appeal, notwithstanding the inactivity; (b) the length of, and reason for the delay; (c) whether the applicant moved diligently to restore the appeal; (d) the merits of the appeal; and (e) any prejudice to the other parties, and whether it can be ameliorated by costs or otherwise. Ultimately the court must decide if restoring the appeal is consistent with the overall interests of justice. In U. (I.B.) v. H. (L.A.), 2016 ABCA 383, 2016 CarswellAlta 2324, Justice Slatter said, at paragraph 10: 10 Factors relevant to deciding whether to restore an appeal include: a. arguable merit to the appeal; b. an explanation for the defect or delay which caused the appeal to be struck; c. reasonable promptness in moving to cure the defect and have the appeal restored to the list; d. intention in time to proceed with the appeal; e. lack of prejudice to the respondents (including considering length of delay). None of these factors is determinative. The failure by the applicant to meet one of them is not fatal because all of the factors are weighed to determine whether it is in the interests of justice to permit the appeal to proceed: Prochazka v Alberta (Maintenance Enforcement Program), 2014 ABCA 448 at para. 4; 707739 Alberta Ltd. v Phillips, 2001 ABCA 219 at para. 13. In Abdi v. Aski Construction Ltd., 2017 ABCA 68, 2017 CarswellAlta 327, the applicants' appeal was struck by the Registrar because the appellants failed to file their factum within the requisite time period. In granting the application to restore the appeal, the Court said: 5 In deciding whether to restore an appeal, this Court considers a number of factors as set out in Prochazka v Alberta (Maintenance Enforcement Program), 2014 ABCA 448 at para 4: (a) arguable merit to the appeal; (b) the explanation for the delay or defect that caused the appeal to be taken off the list; (c) reasonable promptness in moving to cure the defect and have the appeal restored; (d) whether there was a timely intention to proceed with the appeal; and (e) potential prejudice to the respondents (including the length of the delay). None of these factors are determinative; the failure by the applicant to meet one of them is not fatal because all of the factors are weighed to determine whether, overall, it is in the interests of justice to allow the appeal to proceed: 707739 Alberta Ltd v Phillips, 2001 ABCA 219 at para 13, 286 AR 367; Prochazka at para 4; Cox v Howard, 2016 ABCA 311 at para 3. See also Garry v Canada, 2007 ABCA 234 at paras 4-5, 429 AR 292 and the cases cited therein. 6 Where, as here, the appeal was launched in a timely fashion but a subsequent step was inadvertently missed, Cox at para 4 is particularly apt: This logic of recognizing a residual discretion against any strictures in Cairns in favour of condonation of an error as to process delay would seem to apply with even more propriety when the case is one when counsel slips off the rails at an interim step on an existing appeal, and then moves with alacrity to get the appellate train back on the track and there is no harm done. [Emphasis in original] 7 The Rules of Court that set timelines for filing appeal materials subsequent to the notice of appeal are designed to assist in ensuring the appeal proceeds in a timely manner; however, I also agree with the proposition that if an appellant has taken steps to move the appeal forward during the delay, the overall objective of the Rules is not being thwarted: Barker v Sowa, 2003 ABCA 159 at para 3. Further, this Court retains discretion to extend time periods specified in the Rules. In Piikani Nation v. Kostic, 2017 ABCA 350, 2017 CarswellAlta 2914, [2017] A.J. No. 1307, Justice Strekaf said: [19] Rule 14.64 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 directs the Registrar to strike an appeal if the appellant has not filed the Appeal Record and factum within the required time period, or a fast track appeal has not been placed on the hearing list within six months of the filing of the notice of appeal. Once struck, an application must be made to restore the appeal: r 14.65. Although this would have occurred in the ordinary course, these appeals have not been struck. [20] I agree with my colleague Schutz JA who held that the Rules“that set timelines for filing appeal materials subsequent to the notice of appeal are designed to assist in ensuring the appeal proceeds in a timely manner” but “if an appellant has taken steps to move the appeal forward during the delay, the overall objective of the Rules is not being thwarted”: Abdi v Aski Construction Limited, 2017 ABCA 68 at para 7, [2017] A.J. No. 186 (QL). To similar effect, the court may excuse compliance with deadlines and “exercise its discretion to grant the extension in any event” if “there are ‘unique and special circumstances’ and it is in the interests of justice to do so”: Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 109 at para 8, 412 AR 88. See also rules 1.4(2)(h) and 13.5(2). [21] None of the factors considered when exercising the discretion to extend deadlines are prerequisites or determinative, and all are weighed to determine if it is in the interest of justice to permit the appeal to proceed: Prochazka v Alberta (Maintenance Enforcement Program), 2014 ABCA 448 at para 4, [2014] A.J. No. 1439 (QL). [22] In the context of an application for an extension of time to file a factum, the pertinent factors to consider are the reason for the delay, the prospects of moving ahead with the appeal, prejudice to the other party, and the potential merit of the appeal: Keef v Peters, 2015 ABCA 16 at para 6, [2015] A.J. No. 24. Application of those factors to these appeals follows. In C. (C.) v. Alberta (Director of Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act), 2016 ABCA 84, 2016 CarswellAlta 547, Justice Berger said, at paragraph 5: “In my opinion, the prejudicial effect of delay on interested third parties must also be considered.” In Prairie West Homes Inc. v. Baraka Homes Ltd., 2023 ABCA 256, 2023 CarswellAlta 2392, Justice Feehan gave this summary of the applicable law: [10] The test for restoring an appeal is discretionary and engages the following considerations: (a) arguable merit to the appeal; (b) an explanation for the defect or delay which caused the appeal to be taken off the list; (c) reasonable promptness in moving to cure the defect and have the appeal restored to the list; (d) intention in time to proceed with the appeal; and (e) lack of prejudice to the respondents, including the length of delay. None of these factors are determinative. The failure by the applicant to meet one of them is not fatal, because all the factors are weighed to determine whether, overall, it is in the interests of justice to permit the appeal to proceed: Prochazka v Alberta (Maintenance Enforcement Program), 2014 ABCA 448, para 4; Clark v Institute of Chartered Accountants of Alberta (Complaints Inquiry Committee), 2015 ABCA 271, para 5, 607 AR 1. A restoration order may not be in the interests of justice even if all five factors are met: see Warren v Warren, 2019 ABCA 20, para 15, 82 Alta LR (6th) 213. [11] The test for restoring an appeal involves the same considerations whether the appeal has been struck or deemed abandoned: Mylonas v Kadman, 2019 ABCA 39, para 3; Rana v Rana, 2018 ABCA 347, para 8. However, in the case of an appeal deemed abandoned, the threshold for restoration is heightened and the discretion to restore such an appeal is to be “exercised sparingly and always with a view to the interest of justice”: Allen v Alberta (Seniors and Community Supports), 2015 ABCA 238, para 5. [12] Some cases have required “exceptional circumstances over which the appellant had no control [which] made it impossible for the appellant to prosecute the appeal”, “a very onerous obligation that will seldom be discharged”: Scarlett v Wang, 2019 ABCA 72, paras 28, 29. It has been held that when an application to restore is not filed “as soon as reasonably possible”, it must be dismissed: Holden v Holden, 2022 ABCA 341, para 42. [13] Prejudice to the respondent can be assumed, as “at some point the successful party has a legitimate expectation that the judgment is final”: Li v Morgan, 2020 ABCA 186, para 9. 3. Restoration Upon Conditions—Security for Costs In The Owners: Condominium Plan No 982 6403 v. CPI Crown Properties International Corporation, 2018 ABCA 232, 2018 CarswellAlta 1252, Justice Schutz granted an application to restore an appeal to the appeals list. Her Ladyship discussed the imposition of a security for costs order as a condition to the restoration order: 22 An appeal may be restored subject to conditions that are designed to prevent prejudice to the respondents, including that the applicants post security for costs: see Arabian Muslim Association v Canadian Islamic Centre, 2005 ABCA 288 at para 5, 380 AR 179; Cameron Corporation v Edmonton (Subdivision and Development Appeal Board), 2012 ABCA 229 at paras 24–25. 23 Under Rules 14.67 and 4.22, this Court may direct the applicants/cross-respondents to provide security for payment of a costs award: … if the Court considers it just and reasonable to do so, taking into account all of the following: (a) whether it is likely the applicant for the order will be able to enforce an order or judgment against assets in Alberta; (b) the ability of the respondent to the application to pay the costs award; (c) the merits of the action in which the application is filed; (d) whether an order to give security for payment of a costs award would unduly prejudice the respondent's ability to continue the action; (e) any other matter the Court considers appropriate. 24 The cross-applicants bear the onus of proving that these factors weigh in their favour: Aski Construction Ltd v Markos, 2017 ABCA 341 at para 8, [Aski]. … 26 A security for costs order is discretionary. This Court has stated that “[t]he discretion involved … does not require a demonstration that an appeal is doomed. [The Rule] balances the reasonable expectations and rights of parties [to come to] a just and reasonable conclusion”: Haymour v The Owners Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367 at para 8. As set out in DataNet Information Systems Inc v Belzil, 2011 ABCA 40 at paras 3-4, leave to appeal dismissed, 2011 CanLII 60760 (SCC): … At the appeal level, [an appellant's] impecuniosity is a special circumstance supporting an order for security for costs. At the same time, the likely result of granting a security for costs order based, in part, on the special circumstance of impecuniosity of an appellant is that the appellant will not be able to proceed with the appeal. Access to justice does not equate to access to civil processes without fear of costs consequences. Costs are awarded against most unsuccessful civil litigants. The failure to pay costs awarded following trial court process, combined with a demonstrated inability to pay costs should an appeal be unsuccessful is, in most cases, good reason to grant a “security for costs order”. 27 On the other hand, an application for security for costs may be dismissed where it has not been promptly brought and the delay poses a risk of prejudice, especially if the delay is unexplained: Aski at para 9; Collins v Collins (Estate of), 2005 ABCA 41, 363 AR 91 [Collins]; Marathon Canada Limited v Enron Canada Corp, 2008 ABCA 424, 446 AR 88 [Marathon]. The party applying for security for costs is to be prompt in its application so that the appellant may not go on incurring expenses which in the event of being ordered to give security for costs and being unable to find it will be wholly thrown away. Moreover, “security for costs is a remedy to secure that portion of a proceeding that has yet to take place. To hold otherwise is to change the rules after the fact”: Freyburg v Fletcher Challenge Oil and Gas Inc., 2003 ABCA 208 at para 22. These propositions are intended to be a guide for the exercise of the discretion of the Court in making an award. The cross-respondents estimate they have spent $21,600 in preparing appeal documents and urge that the cross-applicants waited approximately seven and one half months after the Notice of Appeal was filed to bring their application. 28 Although this Court has declined to grant security for costs where there has been delay in bringing the application, (for example, Aski at paras 15–18 and Marathon at para 10), where the delays were shorter than here, delay does not invariably defeat the application. In Collins, the application was not made promptly and the respondent had incurred “significant costs.” Despite this, based on the impecuniosity of the respondent, the Court made an order for security for costs for future steps in the appeal: Collins at para 22. 29 This Court recently discussed the role of prejudice in the context of a Rule 4.22 application in Stoney v Trustees for the 1985 Sawridge Trust, 2017 ABCA 437 at para 6, in which it said: Rule 4.22(d) requires consideration of whether a security for costs order “would unduly prejudice the respondent's ability to continue the action”. This criterion is often central to the competing interests that arise in this type of application. On the one hand, the courts are always reluctant to deprive a litigant of his day in court, particularly because of economic hardship. On the other hand, respondents should not be subjected to continuous litigation where they have no prospect of recovering their costs. The presumption in civil procedure that the successful party is entitled to costs acts as an important control on the quantity and intensity of litigation, and that control is missing if the appellant is judgment proof. 30 Where, as here, corporations allege prejudice would result from a security for costs order, they must prove on a balance of probabilities that they have no way of raising money: Calmont Leasing Ltd v 32262 BC Ltd, 2002 ABCA 290 at paras 6–10, 317 AR 331 [Calmont]. “In the case of a limited liability company, it is particularly important that there be sworn evidence that the appellant or plaintiff has no way to raise any kind of security of any description. That is because an impecunious company with a cause of action is a one-way valve which allows money to flow from a successful lawsuit through the company to its creditors or shareholders (or both), but prevents any money from flowing in the opposite direction”: Calmont at para 8. 4. Restoration of a Fast-Track Appeal In Cox v. Howard, 2016 ABCA 311, 2016 CarswellAlta 1983, 45 Alta. L.R. (6th) 24, the appeal was considered as a “fast-track” appeal. As a result of misapprehending the date by which a factum must be filed in a fast-tract appeal, appellant's lawyer was late in filing the appellant's factum, and the appeal was struck. In granting the application to restore the appeal, Justice Watson said: 3 There is no suggestion that the appellant's counsel is insincere in what he is saying. Nor is there any prejudice to respondent from the delay either apparent or asserted. In R v Canto, 2015 ABCA 306 at para 13, 607 AR 298, it was pointed out that the criteria in the famous decision from over eight decades ago, namely Cairns v Cairns, [1931] 4 DLR 819 would not be applied reflexively, let alone counter-intuitively, if it was apparent that on the face of the matter that it would be unjust to deny an extension of time to appeal. In this respect, short term delays tend to be viewed without too much asperity: see eg Grivicic v Alberta Health Services (c.o.b. Tom Baker Cancer Center), 2016 ABCA 47. By comparison, long delays are viewed with less magnanimity: R v Roberge, 2005 SCC 48 at para 7, [2005] 2 SCR 469; Prince Alfred College Incorporated v ADC, [2016] HCA 37. 4 This logic of recognizing a residual discretion against any strictures in Cairns in favour of condonation of an error as to process delay would seem to apply with even more propriety when the case is one when counsel slips off the rails at an interim step on an existing appeal, and then moves with alacrity to get the appellate train back on the track and there is no harm done. If the appeal is also arguable, the Cairns test might be found to be met, quite apart from any residual discretion. 5 A key factor in Cairns was at the heart of Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 109, 412 AR 88 which is a case dealing with extension of time as to the origination of an appeal. The Court examined the record and concluded that the proposed appeal from dismissal of the appellant's action by summary judgment was “hopeless”. This aspect of the Cairns test, namely whether the appeal if it proceeded would have “a reasonable chance of success”, has also been addressed by the material filed for the appellant. Although the respondent contends on analysis of the grounds that this is a fact-grounded decision raising no error in principle nor abuse of discretion, I have concluded that, based on that material, the appellant's arguments are arguable. To what extent they may succeed or fail will be up to a panel. In Warren v. Warren, 2019 ABCA 20, 2019 CarswellAlta 69, Justice Wakeling had before him an application to restore a “fast track” appeal. His Lordship gave this summary of the law: [4] “An appeal may be restored if it is in the interest of justice to do so.”[2] [5] In applying this abstract standard it is helpful to ask a series of questions. [6] First, has the applicant demonstrated an unwavering intention to prosecute the appeal during the period commencing with the last step taken in the appeal process to the date the Registrar struck the appeal? [7] Second, has the applicant provided an explanation for the failure to take the next step on time? Is the explanation consistent with an unwavering intention on the part of the applicant to prosecute the appeal? [8] Third, has the applicant moved with sufficient expedition to cure the defect—by applying for a restoration order and preparing the outstanding documents? [9] Fourth, what are the appeal's prospects of success? Is the appeal frivolous? Is it hopeless? [10] Fifth, will the restoration of the appeal prejudice the respondent to an unacceptable degree? His Lordship also gave this more detailed explanation of the test to be applied: [31] This Court imposes an onerous burden on a party who seeks permission to file an appeal after the appeal period has expired. “The bar must be high and difficult to clear. This Court must send an unequivocal message that time limits are of fundamental importance and must be observed, except in extraordinary circumstances.” This devotion to rule compliance is easily explainable. An unappealed decision is a final disposition and the allocation of burdens and benefits it represents ought to be recognized and enforced. “When the time for appealing has expired, the litigation is at an end; the successful party is entitled to the benefit of the judgment in his or her favour. At this stage, the successful party has a ‘vested right to retain the judgment.’” [32] Slightly different considerations apply when the moving party has filed a notice of appeal and seeks the court's indulgence to cure a post-appeal deficiency. [33] By filing an appeal the appellant has put the nonmoving respondent on notice that the order or judgment that advances the nonmoving party's interests has been challenged and that the nonmoving party must now take this into account in making any future decisions. A prudent party will adjust his or her course of conduct taking into account counsel's assessments of the likelihood the appeal will succeed. [34] If counsel advises the respondent that the likelihood the appeal court will reverse the order or judgment under appeal is very low—perhaps the likelihood the respondent will prevail is twice as high as the likelihood the appellant will succeed—the respondent will not alter course. The respondent will assume that it is safe to proceed on the assumption that the favorable assessment of the respondent's burden or benefits will survive appellate review. But if counsel advises that the likelihood the appeal will be allowed or will be dismissed is the same, the respondent may delay any project that makes sense only if the appeal is dismissed. Proceeding on the assumption that appellate review will not harm the respondent's interests may be foolhardy. [35] For this reason, the burden borne by the moving party is less onerous—but still onerous. [36] The general rule is that an “appeal may be restored if it is in the interest of justice to do so.” [37] This abstract formulation is of marginal, if any, assistance. No court exercising a discretion under the Alberta Rules of Court should adopt a solution that is unfair and unjust. [38] To introduce rationality and consistency a court should consider the queries set out below: In considering whether an application meets this abstract standard, consideration must be given to the following criteria: 1. Is there any reason to conclude that the applicant, at any time after filing the notice of appeal, did not intend to prosecute the appeal? A statement from the applicant that he or she has always intended to prosecute the appeal would, in most cases, be probative. If the court has reason to doubt the applicant's commitment to the appeal, there is no reason to restore it. 2. Has the applicant provided an explanation for the deficiency that prompted the Registrar to strike the appeal? If so, is the explanation consistent with an intention on the part of the appellant to advance the appeal? 3. Has the applicant moved with sufficient expedition to cure the defect, taking into account the nature of the defect? 4. Are there arguable grounds in support of an appeal? Is the likelihood of success high enough to conclude that it is not a frivolous appeal? It makes no sense to breathe life into an appeal that is almost certain to fail. An appeal that is almost certain to fail should be laid to rest without any more private and public resources devoted to it. 5. Will the restoration of the appeal cause the respondent any prejudice? If so, is it appropriate to require the respondent to endure this prejudice? [39] A restoration-of-appeal application that meets the five criteria should be granted in the absence of exceptional circumstances. [40] A restoration application that falls short of one or more of the five criteria should be denied in the absence of exceptional circumstances. There is no reason to restore an appeal that is hopeless. Nor does it make any sense to restore an appeal if the applicant decided at any time to abandon the appeal after filing a notice of appeal. And it is hard to defend a decision to restore an appeal that will impose unreasonable prejudice on the respondent. [footnotes omitted] In Bodnariuk v. Vince, 2023 ABCA 159, 2023 CarswellAlta 1182 at para. 4, Justice Slatter commented on paragraph 31 of Warren v. Warren: [4] The respondent relies on the statement in Warren v Warren, 2019 ABCA 20 at para. 31, 82 Alta LR (6th) 213 that deadlines are only to be extended in “extraordinary circumstances”. The statement quoted in Warren was made with respect to applications to file late appeals, not applications to restore appeals, but even in that context there is little authority for the proposition. Finality of judgments is important, as are the deadlines for prosecuting appeals, but if the test for restoration is met it is not helpful to impose exhortatory limits on the judicial discretion that are not specified in the Rules of Court. As the cases cited in footnote 12 of Warren confirm, the ultimate test is whether it is in the interests of justice to restore the appeal, not whether “extraordinary circumstances” have been shown. The balance of prejudice and convenience between the parties is an important consideration. Also see the annotations under Rule 14.47.

In Warren v.
Warren, 2019 ABCA 20, 2019 CarswellAlta 69, Justice Wakeling had before him an application to restore a “fast track” appeal.

His Lordship gave this summary of the law: [4] “An appeal may be restored if it is in the interest of justice to do so.”[2] [5] In applying this abstract standard it is helpful to ask a series of questions.

[6] First, has the applicant demonstrated an unwavering intention to prosecute the appeal during the period commencing with the last step taken in the appeal process to the date the Registrar struck the appeal?
[7] Second, has the applicant provided an explanation for the failure to take the next step on time?
Is the explanation consistent with an unwavering intention on the part of the applicant to prosecute the appeal?
[8] Third, has the applicant moved with sufficient expedition to cure the defect—by applying for a restoration order and preparing the outstanding documents?
[9] Fourth, what are the appeal's prospects of success?
Is the appeal frivolous?
Is it hopeless?
[10] Fifth, will the restoration of the appeal prejudice the respondent to an unacceptable degree?

His Lordship also gave this more detailed explanation of the test to be applied: [31] This Court imposes an onerous burden on a party who seeks permission to file an appeal after the appeal period has expired. “The bar must be high and difficult to clear.

This Court must send an unequivocal message that time limits are of fundamental importance and must be observed, except in extraordinary circumstances.” This devotion to rule compliance is easily explainable.

An unappealed decision is a final disposition and the allocation of burdens and benefits it represents ought to be recognized and enforced. “When the time for appealing has expired, the litigation is at an end; the successful party is entitled to the benefit of the judgment in his or her favour.

At this stage, the successful party has a ‘vested right to retain the judgment.’” [32] Slightly different considerations apply when the moving party has filed a notice of appeal and seeks the court's indulgence to cure a post-appeal deficiency.

[33] By filing an appeal the appellant has put the nonmoving respondent on notice that the order or judgment that advances the nonmoving party's interests has been challenged and that the nonmoving party must now take this into account in making any future decisions.
A prudent party will adjust his or her course of conduct taking into account counsel's assessments of the likelihood the appeal will succeed.

[34] If counsel advises the respondent that the likelihood the appeal court will reverse the order or judgment under appeal is very low—perhaps the likelihood the respondent will prevail is twice as high as the likelihood the appellant will succeed—the respondent will not alter course.
The respondent will assume that it is safe to proceed on the assumption that the favorable assessment of the respondent's burden or benefits will survive appellate review.
But if counsel advises that the likelihood the appeal will be allowed or will be dismissed is the same, the respondent may delay any project that makes sense only if the appeal is dismissed.
Proceeding on the assumption that appellate review will not harm the respondent's interests may be foolhardy.
[35] For this reason, the burden borne by the moving party is less onerous—but still onerous.
[36] The general rule is that an “appeal may be restored if it is in the interest of justice to do so.” [37] This abstract formulation is of marginal, if any, assistance.
No court exercising a discretion under the Alberta Rules of Court should adopt a solution that is unfair and unjust.

[38] To introduce rationality and consistency a court should consider the queries set out below: In considering whether an application meets this abstract standard, consideration must be given to the following criteria: 1.
Is there any reason to conclude that the applicant, at any time after filing the notice of appeal, did not intend to prosecute the appeal?
A statement from the applicant that he or she has always intended to prosecute the appeal would, in most cases, be probative.
If the court has reason to doubt the applicant's commitment to the appeal, there is no reason to restore it.
Has the applicant provided an explanation for the deficiency that prompted the Registrar to strike the appeal?
If so, is the explanation consistent with an intention on the part of the appellant to advance the appeal?
Has the applicant moved with sufficient expedition to cure the defect, taking into account the nature of the defect?
Are there arguable grounds in support of an appeal?
Is the likelihood of success high enough to conclude that it is not a frivolous appeal?
It makes no sense to breathe life into an appeal that is almost certain to fail.
An appeal that is almost certain to fail should be laid to rest without any more private and public resources devoted to it.
Will the restoration of the appeal cause the respondent any prejudice?
If so, is it appropriate to require the respondent to endure this prejudice?
[39] A restoration-of-appeal application that meets the five criteria should be granted in the absence of exceptional circumstances.
[40] A restoration application that falls short of one or more of the five criteria should be denied in the absence of exceptional circumstances.
There is no reason to restore an appeal that is hopeless.
Nor does it make any sense to restore an appeal if the applicant decided at any time to abandon the appeal after filing a notice of appeal.
And it is hard to defend a decision to restore an appeal that will impose unreasonable prejudice on the respondent.
[footnotes omitted] In Bodnariuk v.
Vince, 2023 ABCA 159, 2023 CarswellAlta 1182 at para.
4, Justice Slatter commented on paragraph 31 of Warren v.
Warren: [4] The respondent relies on the statement in Warren v Warren, 2019 ABCA 20 at para.
31, 82 Alta LR (6th) 213 that deadlines are only to be extended in “extraordinary circumstances”.
The statement quoted in Warren was made with respect to applications to file late appeals, not applications to restore appeals, but even in that context there is little authority for the proposition.

Finality of judgments is important, as are the deadlines for prosecuting appeals, but if the test for restoration is met it is not helpful to impose exhortatory limits on the judicial discretion that are not specified in the Rules of Court.
As the cases cited in footnote 12 of Warren confirm, the ultimate test is whether it is in the interests of justice to restore the appeal, not whether “extraordinary circumstances” have been shown.
The balance of prejudice and convenience between the parties is an important consideration.
Also see the annotations under Rule 14.47.
